questions.name: Network and Perimeter Hacking
questions.keyword: network sniffing concepts passive active promiscuous mode
questions.text: What is 'promiscuous mode' on a network interface, and why is it necessary for passive network sniffing?

answers.text: Promiscuous mode configures the NIC to accept and pass ALL frames on the wire to the OS — regardless of whether the destination MAC address matches the interface's own MAC — enabling packet capture of traffic destined for other hosts
Promiscuous mode disables the network interface's hardware firewall — allowing all packet types including ICMP and UDP that are normally blocked by the NIC
Promiscuous mode enables the network card to transmit at higher speeds — removing rate limiting to increase packet injection throughput during active attacks
Promiscuous mode is a wireless-specific mode that enables monitoring of all 802.11 channels simultaneously — allowing passive capture of all Wi-Fi traffic within range

explanations.a: By default, a NIC in normal mode silently discards frames where the destination MAC address does not match its own MAC or the broadcast address (FF:FF:FF:FF:FF:FF). This prevents the host's CPU from processing traffic destined for other devices. In promiscuous mode, the NIC passes ALL frames seen on the wire/switch port to the operating system — including unicast frames destined for other hosts. Packet capture tools (Wireshark, tcpdump) require promiscuous mode to capture traffic not addressed to the local machine. Setting promiscuous mode: 'ip link set eth0 promisc on' (Linux) or programmatically via libpcap/WinPcap. Note: on switched networks, promiscuous mode only captures traffic on the same switch port without additional techniques (ARP poisoning, port mirroring).
explanations.b: Promiscuous mode does not affect firewall functionality — it modifies how the NIC's hardware MAC address filter processes incoming frames. Hardware firewalls in NICs are a separate subsystem not controlled by promiscuous mode settings.
explanations.c: Promiscuous mode changes the receive filter behavior — it has no effect on transmit speed or rate limiting. Network interface transmission speed is controlled by negotiated link speed (1G, 10G) and the host's packet scheduling, not by the promiscuous mode setting.
explanations.d: Wireless monitor mode (not promiscuous mode) enables passive capture of all 802.11 frames across channels. Promiscuous mode is a generic NIC concept applicable to both wired and wireless interfaces, but the wireless-specific passive capture mode is called 'monitor mode' — configured with 'airmon-ng start wlan0' or 'iw dev wlan0 set type monitor'.

questions.name: Network and Perimeter Hacking
questions.keyword: network sniffing concepts passive active promiscuous mode
questions.text: A penetration tester is on a switched network and wants to capture traffic between a workstation (192.168.1.10) and the default gateway (192.168.1.1). Simply enabling promiscuous mode captures no relevant traffic. Which active sniffing technique MOST directly enables traffic capture in this switched environment?

answers.text: ARP poisoning — sending gratuitous ARP replies to both the workstation and gateway claiming the attacker's MAC is associated with each other's IP, causing both hosts to send traffic through the attacker's machine
Increasing the NIC's buffer size — larger receive buffers allow the NIC to capture additional frames from adjacent switch ports
DNS cache poisoning — redirecting the workstation's DNS queries to the attacker's resolver, which forwards all traffic through the attacker as a DNS proxy
Enabling IPv6 on the attacker's interface — modern switches forward all IPv6 traffic in promiscuous mode regardless of destination MAC addresses

explanations.a: ARP poisoning (ARP spoofing) is the primary active sniffing technique for switched environments: (1) The attacker sends an ARP reply to the workstation (192.168.1.10) claiming MAC:attacker_mac is at IP:192.168.1.1 (the gateway). (2) The attacker sends an ARP reply to the gateway (192.168.1.1) claiming MAC:attacker_mac is at IP:192.168.1.10. (3) Both hosts update their ARP caches with the attacker's MAC for each other's IP. (4) Traffic from the workstation to the gateway is sent to attacker_mac — the attacker captures it, then forwards to the real gateway. (5) Return traffic from the gateway to the workstation similarly routes through the attacker. This creates a Man-in-the-Middle position without requiring any switch configuration access.
explanations.b: NIC buffer size controls how much data can be queued before the OS processes it — it does not affect which frames the switch forwards to the attacker's port. Switches make forwarding decisions based on their MAC address tables, independent of connected hosts' buffer sizes.
explanations.c: DNS cache poisoning redirects hostname resolution — it would cause the workstation to contact a different server for name-resolved connections, but it does not redirect existing IP-addressed traffic between the workstation and its default gateway for non-DNS communication. DNS poisoning cannot intercept IP-layer routing.
explanations.d: IPv6 is a network layer protocol — switches forward IPv6 frames based on destination MAC addresses (learned from Neighbor Discovery, analogous to ARP). Enabling IPv6 on the attacker's interface does not cause switches to send all IPv6 traffic to the attacker's port. This claim is technically incorrect.

questions.name: Network and Perimeter Hacking
questions.keyword: network sniffing concepts passive active promiscuous mode
questions.text: A network administrator wants to monitor all traffic passing through a specific switch port for troubleshooting purposes. Which switch configuration allows a separate monitoring station to passively capture all traffic on that port without being inline in the traffic path?

answers.text: Configure SPAN (Switched Port Analyzer) / port mirroring — the switch copies all frames from the source port (or VLAN) to a designated mirror port where the monitoring station is connected
Configure VTP (VLAN Trunking Protocol) pruning to exclude the monitored port from VLAN updates — VTP pruning redirects all pruned VLAN traffic to the monitoring station
Configure STP (Spanning Tree Protocol) root bridge election on the monitoring station — the root bridge receives all broadcast traffic in the VLAN for analysis
Configure DHCP snooping on the switch — DHCP snooping forwards all client traffic to the DHCP server port where the monitoring station can intercept it

explanations.a: SPAN (Switched Port Analyzer, also called port mirroring) is a switch feature specifically designed for non-intrusive traffic monitoring: (1) Source port(s) or VLAN(s) are defined — the switch copies all frames (ingress, egress, or both) from these sources. (2) Destination port is specified — the monitoring station connects here and receives copied frames. (3) The monitoring station captures all traffic without being inline — the original traffic path is unaffected. (4) Configuration example (Cisco): 'monitor session 1 source interface Gi0/1; monitor session 1 destination interface Gi0/24'. RSPAN (Remote SPAN) extends this across switches using a dedicated VLAN.
explanations.b: VTP pruning optimizes VLAN trunk bandwidth by preventing unnecessary VLAN advertisement floods — it does not redirect traffic to monitoring stations. VTP is a management protocol for VLAN consistency, not a traffic capture mechanism.
explanations.c: The STP root bridge is elected based on bridge priority and MAC address — it is a logical topology role for loop prevention, not a traffic concentration point. Non-root bridges still switch traffic directly between ports without sending it to the root bridge. The root bridge receives topology change notifications, not data plane traffic.
explanations.d: DHCP snooping is a security feature that validates DHCP messages and builds a binding table of trusted client IP-to-MAC mappings — it blocks rogue DHCP servers. DHCP snooping does not redirect client traffic to the DHCP server port for monitoring.

questions.name: Network and Perimeter Hacking
questions.keyword: network sniffing concepts passive active promiscuous mode
questions.text: A security analyst detects unusual network behavior: a host is sending large volumes of ARP replies that were never preceded by ARP requests — updating the ARP caches of multiple hosts on the segment with its own MAC address for many different IP addresses. What attack technique is this, and what is the attacker's likely objective?

answers.text: ARP poisoning / gratuitous ARP flooding — the attacker is associating their MAC address with multiple IP addresses in other hosts' ARP caches, positioning themselves as a Man-in-the-Middle to intercept, read, and forward traffic intended for those IP addresses
The host is performing normal ARP cache maintenance — periodic gratuitous ARP broadcasts are required by the IPv4 specification to keep ARP tables current across all segment hosts
The host is performing ARP proxy service — acting as a network router by responding to ARP queries on behalf of hosts on other network segments that cannot respond directly
The host is conducting a CAM table overflow attack — flooding the switch with ARP frames to exhaust MAC address table capacity and force the switch into hub mode

explanations.a: Unsolicited ARP replies associating one MAC address with multiple IP addresses is the signature of ARP poisoning in progress. The attacker is: (1) Sending gratuitous ARP replies to all segment hosts, claiming their MAC address corresponds to multiple IP addresses (gateway, DNS server, important server IPs). (2) Hosts receive these unsolicited ARP replies and update their ARP caches — now sending traffic for those IP addresses to the attacker's MAC. (3) The attacker receives the intercepted traffic, can read cleartext or decrypt captured sessions, then forwards packets to the real destinations (Man-in-the-Middle). The attacker's objective is traffic interception for credential capture, session hijacking, or data exfiltration.
explanations.b: While gratuitous ARP (unsolicited ARP replies announcing a host's own IP-to-MAC mapping) is a legitimate technique for IP conflict detection and cluster failover, the described behavior — large volumes of ARP replies updating caches with the attacker's MAC for MANY different IP addresses — is not normal operational behavior. Legitimate gratuitous ARPs are infrequent and only announce the sending host's own IP address.
explanations.c: ARP proxy (proxy ARP) is a legitimate network device feature where a router responds to ARP queries for hosts on other network segments — allowing cross-subnet communication without gateway configuration. Proxy ARP is a deliberate router configuration, not a flooding behavior, and the router's MAC is only provided for specific legitimate IP routes, not for large numbers of unrelated IPs.
explanations.d: CAM table overflow attacks use fake source MAC addresses (not fake ARP source IP mappings) to fill the switch's MAC address table. CAM overflow uses tools that generate frames with random source MACs — not ARP reply content associating one specific MAC with multiple IPs. ARP poisoning and CAM overflow are distinct attack techniques with different mechanisms and packet structures.

questions.name: Network and Perimeter Hacking
questions.keyword: MAC flooding CAM table overflow switch security
questions.text: How does a MAC flooding attack work against a network switch, and what is the result when the CAM table is exhausted?

answers.text: MAC flooding sends frames with thousands of unique fake source MAC addresses, exhausting the switch's Content Addressable Memory (CAM) table — when full, many switches fail open and flood all frames out all ports (behaving like a hub), enabling passive sniffing
MAC flooding fills the switch's CPU cache with fake MAC addresses, causing the switch to crash and reboot — creating a temporary network outage for denial-of-service purposes
MAC flooding sends malformed frames with invalid MAC addresses, causing the switch's frame processing ASIC to generate error interrupts that crash the forwarding engine
MAC flooding rapidly cycles the same MAC address across different switch ports, confusing the MAC learning algorithm and preventing legitimate frames from being forwarded

explanations.a: A MAC flooding attack (using tools like macof from the dsniff suite) sends frames with randomly generated fake source MAC addresses at high volume. The switch learns each new source MAC, adding it to the CAM table. When the CAM table reaches capacity, the switch can no longer learn new legitimate MAC-to-port mappings. Many switches (particularly older models) respond by 'failing open' — flooding frames for unknown destination MACs out all ports, converting from unicast switching to hub-like broadcasting. An attacker connected to any switch port can now capture all traffic in the VLAN using promiscuous mode.
explanations.b: MAC flooding primarily targets the CAM (Content Addressable Memory) table — the switch's hardware forwarding database that maps MAC addresses to switch ports. While CAM table exhaustion can impact CPU performance (as the switch falls back to software forwarding), the primary attack goal is causing fail-open flooding behavior, not switch reboot.
explanations.c: Frame format errors (invalid checksums, undersized/oversized frames) are handled by the switch's hardware error detection — malformed frames are discarded at the physical layer without reaching the MAC learning process. CAM table overflow requires valid-looking frames with many unique source MAC addresses, not invalid frame formats.
explanations.d: Moving the same MAC address between ports rapidly does confuse the MAC learning process (MAC flapping) but this is a different attack scenario (potentially related to STP manipulation). MAC flooding specifically uses thousands of different fake MAC addresses simultaneously to fill CAM table capacity, not cycling one MAC address.

questions.name: Network and Perimeter Hacking
questions.keyword: MAC flooding CAM table overflow switch security
questions.text: A network engineer wants to prevent MAC flooding attacks on access layer switches. Which Cisco switch security feature directly limits the number of MAC addresses learned on each port?

answers.text: Port Security — configures a maximum number of MAC addresses per port and defines violation actions (protect, restrict, shutdown) when the limit is exceeded
802.1Q VLAN tagging — limiting VLANs to one MAC address per port prevents CAM table overflow by enforcing strict per-VLAN MAC uniqueness
DHCP Snooping — validates DHCP transactions and limits the number of IP addresses per port, indirectly preventing MAC address proliferation
Dynamic ARP Inspection (DAI) — validates ARP packets against the DHCP snooping binding table, limiting the MAC addresses that can perform ARP resolution per port

explanations.a: Cisco Port Security is specifically designed to prevent MAC flooding by limiting MAC address learning per port: (1) 'switchport port-security maximum 1' limits the port to 1 MAC address (for end-user access ports). (2) 'switchport port-security violation shutdown' disables the port if the limit is exceeded (most secure). (3) Alternative violations: 'restrict' (drops violating frames, sends SNMP trap) and 'protect' (silently drops violating frames). (4) 'switchport port-security mac-address sticky' dynamically learns and persists the first MAC seen. When macof generates thousands of fake MACs on a port with port-security maximum 1, the first fake MAC triggers a violation and the port shuts down — protecting other ports from the overflow attack.
explanations.b: 802.1Q VLAN tagging is a frame encapsulation standard for carrying VLAN membership information across trunk links — it does not control the number of MAC addresses learned per switch port. 802.1Q has no per-port MAC limiting functionality.
explanations.c: DHCP Snooping validates DHCP message types (only allowing server responses from trusted uplink ports) and builds a binding table of IP-to-MAC-to-port mappings — it does not directly limit the number of MAC addresses learned by the switch's CAM table or prevent MAC flooding.
explanations.d: Dynamic ARP Inspection validates ARP packets against the DHCP snooping binding database — it prevents ARP poisoning by dropping ARP replies that don't match the binding table. DAI does not limit the number of MAC addresses learned per port or prevent MAC flooding attacks.

questions.name: Network and Perimeter Hacking
questions.keyword: MAC flooding CAM table overflow switch security
questions.text: An attacker performs a successful MAC flooding attack on a switch, causing it to fail open and flood all frames. The attacker captures all traffic on the VLAN. A security analyst reviews the switch logs and finds Event ID alerts. Which log entry MOST specifically indicates a MAC flooding attack was in progress?

answers.text: 'STP topology change detected on VLAN 10' — topology changes are caused by MAC flooding disrupting the spanning tree root bridge election
'Interface Gi0/5 error-disabled: duplex mismatch detected' — duplex mismatches are caused by the physical disruption from MAC flooding frame injection
'DHCP lease exhaustion: address pool depleted on subnet 192.168.1.0/24' — DHCP pool exhaustion always accompanies successful MAC flooding attacks
'Port Gi0/5 security violation: MAC address count exceeded maximum of 3, action: restrict' — repeated port security violations with rapidly changing MAC addresses indicate MAC flooding activity

explanations.a: STP topology changes are triggered by port state changes (ports going up or down, root bridge changes) — not by MAC flooding. MAC flooding does cause CAM table churn but doesn't directly generate STP topology change notifications. An STP topology change during a MAC flooding attack would be a secondary effect of disruption, not a primary indicator.
explanations.b: Duplex mismatches occur when one end of a link negotiates half-duplex and the other negotiates full-duplex — typically a cable or auto-negotiation issue. Duplex mismatches cause late collisions and reduced throughput but are completely unrelated to MAC flooding attacks and their software-generated frames.
explanations.c: DHCP lease exhaustion is caused by DHCP starvation attacks (sending DHCP Discover frames with fake MAC addresses to exhaust the IP address pool) — a separate but related attack that can be combined with MAC flooding but is not a log indicator of MAC flooding itself. MAC flooding does not directly consume DHCP leases.
explanations.d: Port security violation alerts are the direct indicator of MAC flooding: when port-security is configured with a maximum MAC count (e.g., maximum 3) and macof generates thousands of fake MAC addresses on that port, repeated 'MAC address count exceeded maximum' violations appear in logs for that port. High frequency of violation events from a single port within seconds is a distinctive MAC flooding signature. The 'restrict' action logs each violation while continuing to forward legitimate traffic from learned MACs.

questions.name: Network and Perimeter Hacking
questions.keyword: MAC flooding CAM table overflow switch security
questions.text: A security researcher evaluates two switch security controls against MAC flooding: Port Security (with maximum 2 MACs per port) vs. 802.1X Network Access Control. Against a sophisticated attacker who can generate exactly 2 unique fake MAC addresses per port before moving to adjacent ports, which control is MORE robust and why?

answers.text: Port Security is more robust — limiting MACs to 2 per port mathematically prevents all MAC flooding regardless of attacker sophistication, since 2 MAC addresses cannot flood a CAM table
Both controls are equally robust — port security and 802.1X provide identical protection mechanisms that respond identically to sophisticated MAC flooding evasion techniques
Neither control provides meaningful protection — MAC flooding is exclusively a physical layer attack that cannot be prevented by Layer 2 switch security features

802.1X NAC is more robust — port security's maximum 2 MACs per port can still be evaded by an attacker who generates exactly 2 fake addresses per port; 802.1X requires cryptographic authentication of each device before any MAC is learned, preventing unauthorized devices from sending frames that populate the CAM table regardless of MAC count manipulation

explanations.a: Port Security with maximum 2 MACs per port is still vulnerable to a sophisticated attacker who generates exactly 2 fake MACs per port across many ports. If the switch has 48 ports, an attacker with access to multiple ports can generate 2×48=96 fake MACs — still potentially filling a CAM table with many hundreds of entries. Additionally, if the attacker targets a VLAN spanning multiple switches, the scale multiplies. 2 MACs per port reduces but doesn't eliminate the flooding vector.
explanations.b: Port Security and 802.1X operate through completely different mechanisms: Port Security counts MAC addresses post-admission; 802.1X prevents admission without authentication. Against an attacker who can precisely control MAC count, 802.1X provides strong protection while Port Security provides weaker protection. They are not equivalent in this threat scenario.
explanations.c: MAC flooding is a Layer 2 attack, and Layer 2 switch security features (Port Security, 802.1X, 802.1AE MACsec) are specifically designed to prevent it. These are not Layer 1 physical controls — they operate in the switch's forwarding plane and authentication stack. Layer 2 security features are the appropriate and effective countermeasure.
explanations.d: 802.1X (IEEE 802.1X Port-Based Network Access Control) requires cryptographic EAP authentication before a port is authorized to pass data traffic: (1) When a device connects, the switch sends an EAP-Request to the supplicant (connecting device). (2) The device must authenticate using valid credentials (certificate, username/password via RADIUS). (3) Until authentication succeeds, the port is in 'unauthorized' state — no frames from the device are forwarded or learned into the CAM table. (4) An attacker cannot generate ANY MAC addresses into the CAM table without valid credentials, regardless of how many fake MACs they generate. 802.1X prevents unauthorized frame injection at the authentication level, making MAC flooding impossible for unauthenticated devices — a fundamentally stronger control than count-based limiting.

questions.name: Network and Perimeter Hacking
questions.keyword: ARP spoofing poisoning MITM man-in-the-middle
questions.text: ARP (Address Resolution Protocol) has a fundamental design weakness that enables ARP poisoning attacks. What is this weakness?

answers.text: ARP uses TCP for transport, which allows attackers to inject forged segments into the reliable delivery stream
ARP operates at Layer 7 (Application layer), allowing web-based scripts to forge ARP replies through browser JavaScript execution
ARP requires administrative privileges to operate, which attackers exploit by escalating to root before sending spoofed replies
ARP has no authentication mechanism — any host can send an ARP reply claiming any IP-to-MAC mapping, and receiving hosts accept and cache these replies without verifying their authenticity

explanations.a: ARP operates at Layer 2 (Data Link layer) and uses Ethernet frames directly — it does not use TCP, UDP, or IP. ARP predates TCP/IP and is a Layer 2 protocol that resolves IP addresses to MAC addresses within a network segment. There is no TCP transport layer involvement.
explanations.b: ARP operates at Layer 2 (Data Link layer) — it is a hardware-level protocol processed by the network stack before IP, TCP, or application layers. Browser JavaScript has no access to Layer 2 operations — browsers operate at Layer 7 through system networking APIs. ARP cannot be manipulated through web scripting.
explanations.c: ARP operates at the kernel networking stack level — standard user-space tools can send ARP packets using raw socket APIs without requiring root privileges in some configurations, and with typical privilege levels in others. Administrative privilege is a practical requirement for raw socket access, not an ARP protocol design weakness.
explanations.d: ARP (RFC 826, 1982) was designed for trusted network environments with no authentication requirement. ARP has no mechanism to verify that the sender of an ARP reply is the legitimate owner of the claimed IP address. When a host receives an ARP reply — whether solicited or unsolicited (gratuitous) — it simply updates its ARP cache with the MAC-IP mapping in the reply without any validation. This allows any host on the local segment to: (1) Send an unsolicited ARP reply claiming 'IP 192.168.1.1 is at MAC aa:bb:cc:dd:ee:ff' (the attacker's MAC). (2) All receiving hosts update their ARP caches. (3) Traffic for 192.168.1.1 is sent to the attacker's MAC. The design assumption was that all hosts on the local network were trusted — a false assumption in modern environments.

questions.name: Network and Perimeter Hacking
questions.keyword: ARP spoofing poisoning MITM man-in-the-middle
questions.text: An attacker uses Ettercap to perform ARP poisoning between a victim (192.168.1.20) and the default gateway (192.168.1.1). After establishing the MITM position, the attacker wants to capture HTTP credentials. Which additional step is REQUIRED for the attacker to capture cleartext credentials from HTTPS traffic?

answers.text: No additional step is required — MITM position through ARP poisoning automatically decrypts HTTPS traffic because the attacker controls the Layer 2 forwarding path
The attacker must redirect the victim to an HTTP mirror of the HTTPS site using DNS poisoning — ARP poisoning cannot be combined with HTTPS interception
The attacker must install a packet capture agent on the victim's workstation — MITM position only captures traffic metadata, not payload content

The attacker must perform SSL stripping (sslstrip) or present a fraudulent TLS certificate to the victim's browser — HTTPS encryption prevents credential capture even from a MITM position without active TLS interception

explanations.a: MITM position through ARP poisoning intercepts Layer 2 frames — but HTTPS encrypts the HTTP payload with TLS at Layer 5-7. An attacker in MITM position sees the TCP stream but sees only ciphertext within the TLS record. The attacker cannot decrypt TLS-encrypted credentials without actively terminating the TLS session, which requires certificate presentation and would trigger browser warnings if done with an untrusted certificate.
explanations.b: ARP poisoning and DNS poisoning are complementary techniques that can be combined, but the statement that 'ARP poisoning cannot be combined with HTTPS interception' is incorrect. Both techniques can be combined — ARP poisoning establishes the MITM position, and SSL stripping (which can be launched from the MITM position) downgrades HTTPS connections. The combination is a well-documented attack pattern.
explanations.c: ARP poisoning with packet forwarding gives the attacker complete access to forwarded packet payloads — this is the entire point of MITM positioning. The attacker sees full frame content of all non-encrypted traffic. Credentials traveling over HTTP (port 80) are visible; HTTPS credentials are encrypted.
explanations.d: HTTPS (HTTP over TLS) encrypts all HTTP content including credentials and cookies between the client and the TLS termination point. A MITM who only intercepts Layer 2 frames sees encrypted TLS records — useless without the TLS session keys. Active TLS interception requires: (1) SSL stripping (sslstrip) — downgrades HTTPS to HTTP by intercepting the initial HTTP connection and serving HTTP, while maintaining the HTTPS connection to the real server. The victim sees HTTP; the attacker sees cleartext. Defeated by HSTS preloading and browsers that refuse HTTP on HSTS domains. (2) TLS proxy with fraudulent certificate — presents a forged certificate to the victim's browser. The browser shows a certificate warning unless the attacker's CA certificate is in the victim's trust store.

questions.name: Network and Perimeter Hacking
questions.keyword: ARP spoofing poisoning MITM man-in-the-middle
questions.text: Which Linux command sends a gratuitous ARP reply claiming that IP 192.168.1.1 has MAC address 00:11:22:33:44:55 — useful for ARP poisoning the target 192.168.1.50's ARP cache?

answers.text: arping -A -s 00:11:22:33:44:55 -I eth0 192.168.1.1 — sends gratuitous ARP announcements from the specified source MAC
nmap --script arp-spoof 192.168.1.50 --gateway 192.168.1.1 — Nmap's built-in ARP spoofing script poisons the target's ARP cache
arp -s 192.168.1.1 00:11:22:33:44:55 — adds a static ARP entry to the local kernel ARP table for the gateway IP
arpspoof -i eth0 -t 192.168.1.50 192.168.1.1 — tells target 192.168.1.50 that 192.168.1.1 is at the attacker's MAC address (from the dsniff suite)

explanations.a: arping -A sends gratuitous ARP announcements to update caches on the local network, and with -s can specify source MAC. However, arping -A sends ARP to broadcast (all hosts), not specifically targeting 192.168.1.50's cache. It is also typically used for legitimate IP conflict detection, not specifically targeted ARP poisoning of one host.
explanations.b: Nmap does not have an 'arp-spoof' script — Nmap's NSE library includes ARP-related scripts for discovery (arp-ping) but not ARP spoofing. ARP poisoning is not part of Nmap's scanning functionality. Nmap is a network scanner, not an attack framework for Layer 2 poisoning.
explanations.c: 'arp -s' adds a static ARP entry to the LOCAL system's ARP table — it affects only the attacker's own machine, not the target's ARP cache. This command has no network transmission and cannot poison other hosts' caches.
explanations.d: arpspoof (from the dsniff suite) is the standard tool for targeted ARP poisoning: 'arpspoof -i eth0 -t 192.168.1.50 192.168.1.1' sends ARP replies to 192.168.1.50 (-t target) claiming that 192.168.1.1 (the spoofed IP) is at the attacker's MAC address. The attacker's actual MAC (from eth0) replaces the legitimate gateway MAC in 192.168.1.50's ARP cache. To complete the MITM (bidirectional interception), a second arpspoof command is run in the other direction: 'arpspoof -i eth0 -t 192.168.1.1 192.168.1.50' — poisoning the gateway's cache too.

questions.name: Network and Perimeter Hacking
questions.keyword: ARP spoofing poisoning MITM man-in-the-middle
questions.text: An organization deploys Dynamic ARP Inspection (DAI) on their switches to prevent ARP poisoning. A security auditor reviews the DAI configuration and finds it's enabled only on access ports but not on trunk uplinks. Why is this configuration correct, and what would happen if DAI were enabled on trunk uplinks without proper trust configuration?

answers.text: DAI should be enabled on trunk ports only — access ports are trusted by design since only authorized workstations connect to access ports
The configuration is incorrect — DAI must be enabled identically on all port types (access and trunk) without distinction for it to provide any security benefit
DAI should be disabled on all ports — ARP inspection creates processing overhead that degrades switch performance unacceptably for production environments

Trunk ports should be configured as DAI-trusted interfaces — enabling DAI on trunk uplinks without trust configuration causes DAI to drop legitimate ARP frames from upstream routers, switches, and DHCP servers that are not in the DAI binding table, breaking valid network connectivity

explanations.a: Access ports are NOT trusted by design — they connect to end-user workstations and untrusted client devices. ARP poisoning is typically launched from compromised workstations on access ports. DAI's primary function is validating ARP from untrusted access ports against the DHCP snooping binding table.
explanations.b: The correct DAI deployment specifically distinguishes access ports (untrusted — DAI validates ARP) from trunk uplinks (trusted — DAI passes ARP without validation). Applying identical configuration to all port types would either: break valid connectivity on trunk ports (if all are untrusted) or provide no protection on access ports (if all are trusted). The distinction is fundamental to correct DAI operation.
explanations.c: DAI processing overhead on modern switches is negligible — switches are specifically designed for high-speed frame processing including ARP inspection. ARP frames represent a tiny fraction of total network traffic. Performance impact from DAI is not a practical concern for production environments.
explanations.d: Dynamic ARP Inspection validates ARP packets on untrusted ports by checking whether the ARP sender's IP-to-MAC mapping matches the DHCP snooping binding table. Trunk uplinks (connecting to routers, upstream switches, servers with static IPs) send legitimate ARP frames that may not have entries in the DHCP snooping binding table (because these devices use static IPs or are DHCP servers themselves, not DHCP clients). If DAI is enabled on trunk ports without 'ip arp inspection trust', DAI drops their ARP frames as 'invalid', breaking router connectivity and server ARP resolution. Correct configuration: 'ip arp inspection trust' on trunk uplinks and DHCP server ports; 'ip arp inspection' (untrusted, default) on access ports only.

questions.name: Network and Perimeter Hacking
questions.keyword: DHCP starvation rogue DHCP server attack
questions.text: A DHCP starvation attack exhausts a DHCP server's address pool. What is the MOST common subsequent step attackers take after successfully starving the legitimate DHCP server?

answers.text: The attacker immediately disconnects from the network — the goal of DHCP starvation is purely denial-of-service to prevent new devices from obtaining IP addresses
The attacker exploits the DHCP server's crashed state to gain root shell access — DHCP pool exhaustion causes a buffer overflow in the DHCP service that the attacker exploits for RCE
The attacker uses the exhausted IP pool to perform BGP route injection — DHCP pool exhaustion grants the attacker BGP routing privileges on the network segment

The attacker deploys a rogue DHCP server — when the legitimate DHCP server cannot allocate addresses (pool exhausted), clients receive responses from the rogue server that configures them with the attacker's gateway IP for MITM positioning

explanations.a: DHCP starvation alone is a denial-of-service attack preventing IP assignment — useful for disruption, but attackers typically combine it with a rogue DHCP server for active MITM positioning. Pure DoS is the fallback goal; the more impactful attack uses the starvation as setup for rogue DHCP deployment.
explanations.b: DHCP pool exhaustion is a resource exhaustion attack (logical, not memory-based) — filling up the IP address pool by consuming all available leases. This does not cause buffer overflows or code execution vulnerabilities in properly implemented DHCP servers. The DHCP server continues running but simply has no available addresses to allocate.
explanations.c: BGP (Border Gateway Protocol) route injection requires BGP session establishment with a peering router — it has no relationship to DHCP pool exhaustion. DHCP operates at Layer 7 for IP address assignment; BGP operates at Layer 4 for inter-AS routing. These are completely separate protocols.
explanations.d: The combined DHCP starvation + rogue DHCP server attack sequence: (1) DHCP starvation — the attacker sends many DHCP Discover requests with randomized source MAC addresses using tools like dhcpstarv or yersinia. The legitimate DHCP server allocates addresses for each fake request until its pool is exhausted. (2) Rogue DHCP deployment — the attacker runs a rogue DHCP server that responds to new client DHCP Discover requests (which the legitimate server can no longer answer). (3) Malicious configuration — the rogue DHCP server provides: clients' IP addresses, but configures the default gateway as the attacker's IP and the DNS server as the attacker's IP. (4) MITM and DNS poisoning — clients route all traffic through the attacker (gateway MITM) and resolve all hostnames through the attacker's DNS (enabling DNS-based phishing).

questions.name: Network and Perimeter Hacking
questions.keyword: DHCP starvation rogue DHCP server attack
questions.text: Which switch security feature prevents rogue DHCP servers from responding to client DHCP requests on untrusted switch ports?

answers.text: Port Security — limits MAC addresses per port, preventing rogue DHCP servers from sending responses with multiple IP leases
Storm Control — rate-limits DHCP broadcast traffic to prevent the rogue DHCP server from flooding the network with unauthorized OFFER packets
Dynamic ARP Inspection — validates ARP packets from DHCP servers to prevent them from poisoning client ARP caches with rogue gateway addresses
DHCP Snooping — classifies switch ports as trusted (uplinks to legitimate DHCP servers) or untrusted (access ports), dropping DHCP server responses (OFFER, ACK) received on untrusted ports

explanations.a: Port Security limits the number of MAC addresses learned per port — it does not inspect or filter DHCP message types. A rogue DHCP server sending responses from a single MAC address would not trigger port security violations.
explanations.b: Storm Control rate-limits broadcast, multicast, or unknown unicast traffic to prevent flooding that degrades network performance. While DHCP uses broadcast, storm control does not differentiate DHCP message types (client vs. server) — it would rate-limit all DHCP traffic indiscriminately. Storm control is not a security control for preventing rogue DHCP servers.
explanations.c: Dynamic ARP Inspection validates ARP packet authenticity by checking against the DHCP snooping binding table — it prevents ARP poisoning but does not specifically block rogue DHCP server responses. DAI operates after DHCP assignment, not during the DHCP exchange.
explanations.d: DHCP Snooping is specifically designed to prevent rogue DHCP servers: (1) Switch ports are classified as trusted (uplinks to DHCP servers, router interfaces) or untrusted (all access ports where clients connect). (2) DHCP server messages (DHCPOFFER, DHCPACK, DHCPNAK) are only permitted on trusted ports. (3) If a DHCP server message arrives on an untrusted port (where a rogue DHCP server is connected), the switch drops the frame. (4) Client messages (DHCPDISCOVER, DHCPREQUEST) are permitted on untrusted ports. (5) The DHCP snooping binding table records legitimate IP-to-MAC-to-port mappings for use by DAI. Cisco configuration: 'ip dhcp snooping; ip dhcp snooping vlan 10; interface Gi0/24 (uplink); ip dhcp snooping trust'.

questions.name: Network and Perimeter Hacking
questions.keyword: DHCP starvation rogue DHCP server attack
questions.text: A penetration tester uses the tool 'yersinia -G' (graphical mode) for DHCP attacks. The tester wants to exhaust the DHCP pool on the 192.168.10.0/24 network. Which yersinia attack achieves this?

answers.text: DHCP ACK — the tester sends fake DHCP acknowledgments to all hosts, causing them to use incorrect IP addresses
DHCP DECLINE flooding — sending DHCP Decline messages for addresses not in use causes the DHCP server to mark all addresses as 'declined' and exclude them from future allocation

DHCP DISCOVER flooding — sending thousands of DHCP Discover packets with unique, randomized source MAC addresses causes the DHCP server to allocate and hold leases for each fake request until the pool is exhausted
DHCP RELEASE flooding — the tester sends DHCP Release messages for all active leases, causing legitimate hosts to lose their IP addresses simultaneously

explanations.a: Sending fake DHCP ACK messages from the attacker's position (not being the actual DHCP server) would not be accepted by clients — clients only process ACK messages from the DHCP server they sent a REQUEST to, identified by the xid (transaction ID) matching their prior request. Forging ACKs without coordinating with legitimate DHCP transactions would be ineffective.
explanations.b: DHCP DECLINE is sent by a client when it discovers a conflict with the offered IP address (via ARP verification). Flooding DECLINE messages would mark those specific offered IPs as unavailable, but the attack requires first receiving OFFER responses — meaning some addresses are consumed. This is a slower, less efficient starvation technique than DISCOVER flooding.
explanations.c: DHCP starvation via DISCOVER flooding: the DHCP protocol assigns a lease when a server receives a DHCPDISCOVER (discover new address), responds with DHCPOFFER, receives DHCPREQUEST, and sends DHCPACK. For starvation, the attacker typically sends only DHCPDISCOVER with unique source MACs — the server responds with DHCPOFFERs and tentatively reserves addresses. If the attacker then sends DHCPREQUEST, the server fully allocates the lease for the fake MAC. Yersinia's 'DHCP DISCOVER' attack sends thousands of Discovers with random MACs, exhausting the server's address pool through allocation. Each fake MAC receives a lease that expires only after the lease timeout (often 24 hours or more).
explanations.d: DHCP RELEASE messages release leases, causing hosts to lose IP connectivity until they renegotiate. While this is a disruptive attack, it is not pool exhaustion — releasing leases makes addresses available for legitimate reassignment. The attack denies service to current holders but doesn't exhaust the pool itself.

questions.name: Network and Perimeter Hacking
questions.keyword: DHCP starvation rogue DHCP server attack
questions.text: After a DHCP starvation + rogue DHCP attack, clients receive the attacker's IP (192.168.1.99) as their default gateway. The attacker must ensure traffic is forwarded to the legitimate gateway (192.168.1.1) or clients will notice connectivity problems. Which operating system setting MUST the attacker enable, and why?

answers.text: The attacker must enable firewall packet logging — logging all forwarded frames enables the attacker to capture credentials without clients noticing latency increases
The attacker must enable TCP timestamps — timestamps ensure that forwarded packets maintain correct sequence numbers, preventing TCP session failures during interception

The attacker must enable IP forwarding (net.ipv4.ip_forward=1 on Linux) — without this, the attacker's host drops intercepted packets rather than forwarding them to the real gateway, causing clients to lose internet connectivity and revealing the attack through widespread connectivity failure
The attacker must enable promiscuous mode on their network interface — without promiscuous mode, the attacker's NIC drops packets from clients before they can be forwarded to the gateway

explanations.a: Firewall packet logging captures metadata about forwarded frames for logging purposes — it does not affect packet forwarding behavior. Enabling logging would not cause intercepted packets to be forwarded to the real gateway.
explanations.b: TCP timestamps (RFC 1323) improve TCP performance through better RTT estimation and protection against sequence number wraparound in high-speed connections. TCP timestamps have no impact on packet forwarding behavior between networks. TCP sequence numbers are maintained per-connection endpoint and are not modified by intermediate routers.
explanations.c: IP forwarding is the kernel setting that enables an OS to function as a router — accepting packets destined for IP addresses other than its own and forwarding them toward their destination. By default, Linux (and most operating systems) drops packets not addressed to the local host. When clients route traffic through the attacker's IP (192.168.1.99) as their gateway: (1) Without ip_forward enabled: The attacker's OS receives the client's packet (e.g., destined for 8.8.8.8), declines to forward it (IP is not local), and drops it. The client's connection times out — all internet connectivity breaks. Users notice immediately. (2) With ip_forward enabled ('echo 1 > /proc/sys/net/ipv4/ip_forward'): The attacker's OS acts as a router — it inspects the packet (reads/captures credentials), then forwards it to the real gateway (192.168.1.1). Traffic flows normally from the client's perspective, maintaining the covert MITM position.
explanations.d: Promiscuous mode enables the NIC to pass frames with any destination MAC to the OS — it affects which frames the NIC delivers to the OS, not whether the OS forwards received packets. When clients have the attacker's MAC as their gateway (from rogue DHCP), frames are sent with destination MAC = attacker's MAC — the NIC receives these in normal mode (no promiscuous mode needed) since they ARE addressed to the attacker. Promiscuous mode is for capturing frames addressed to OTHER hosts, not for receiving frames correctly addressed to the attacker.

questions.name: Network and Perimeter Hacking
questions.keyword: DNS poisoning spoofing cache Kaminsky attack
questions.text: DNS cache poisoning injects false DNS records into a resolver's cache. Which landmark 2008 vulnerability (discovered by Dan Kaminsky) dramatically increased DNS cache poisoning attack feasibility?

answers.text: The BGP route hijacking vulnerability — Kaminsky discovered that DNS poisoning could be combined with BGP route injection to redirect internet traffic at a global scale
The DNSSEC implementation bug — Kaminsky discovered that DNSSEC signatures could be forged using MD5 collision attacks, enabling authenticated DNS record injection

The DNS source port randomization weakness — before Kaminsky's research, DNS resolvers used predictable or fixed source ports for outgoing queries, dramatically reducing the search space for forging DNS responses and poisoning resolver caches
The TTL overflow vulnerability — Kaminsky showed that setting artificially high TTL values caused resolvers to cache poisoned records permanently

explanations.a: Kaminsky's 2008 research was specifically about DNS cache poisoning through source port prediction — not BGP route hijacking. BGP security is a separate research area. Kaminsky's work focused entirely on the DNS protocol's implementation weaknesses.
explanations.b: DNSSEC uses RSA, ECDSA, or similar algorithms — not MD5. MD5 collision attacks are unrelated to DNSSEC signature forgery. Kaminsky's research preceded widespread DNSSEC deployment and was not about DNSSEC implementation bugs.
explanations.c: Dan Kaminsky's landmark 2008 DNS research (coordinated disclosure with DNS vendors before publication) revealed that DNS resolvers using predictable or limited source port ranges for outbound DNS queries created a dramatically small search space for off-path DNS response forgery: (1) DNS uses a 16-bit transaction ID (TXID) — 65,536 possibilities. (2) Before Kaminsky: many resolvers used port 53 as source port for all queries, or small ranges, reducing the additional randomization space. (3) The attack: an off-path attacker races to send forged DNS responses with guessed TXID before the legitimate response arrives. With low source port entropy, the attacker could try all combinations in seconds. (4) Kaminsky showed that by querying for random subdomains of the target domain repeatedly, the attacker could get many TXID guesses per poisoning attempt, dramatically accelerating the race. (5) Fix: mandate full source port randomization (RFC 5452) — adding 16 bits of port randomness increases the search space to ~4 billion.
explanations.d: DNS TTL (Time to Live) controls how long records are cached before expiry — high TTL values cause longer caching periods, but TTL overflow is not a defined vulnerability class from Kaminsky's research. The Kaminsky attack was about TXID and source port prediction enabling cache poisoning, not TTL manipulation.

questions.name: Network and Perimeter Hacking
questions.keyword: DNS poisoning spoofing cache Kaminsky attack
questions.text: An attacker successfully poisons the DNS resolver cache used by a corporate network, replacing the A record for 'corp-vpn.targetorg.com' with the attacker's IP (198.51.100.10). When employees connect to the VPN, what attack does this enable?

answers.text: The attacker gains administrative access to the legitimate VPN server — DNS poisoning grants read/write access to the DNS-hijacked server's configuration

The attacker can present a credential-harvesting fake VPN portal to employees who navigate to corp-vpn.targetorg.com — their browsers resolve to the attacker's server, which mimics the VPN login page to capture credentials
The DNS poisoning has no practical attack value — VPN clients validate server identity through IP address verification rather than DNS hostname resolution
The attacker automatically obtains a valid TLS certificate for corp-vpn.targetorg.com from any certificate authority — DNS control grants automatic certificate issuance privileges

explanations.a: DNS poisoning redirects hostname resolution to the attacker's IP — it does not grant any access to the legitimate server at its real IP address. The attacker controls what their own server (198.51.100.10) does, not the legitimate VPN server.
explanations.b: DNS poisoning enables credential phishing through hostname hijacking: (1) Employees type or click 'corp-vpn.targetorg.com' in their VPN client or browser. (2) Their DNS resolver (poisoned) returns 198.51.100.10 (attacker's server) instead of the real VPN server IP. (3) The attacker's server presents a convincing replica of the VPN login portal. (4) If HTTPS is not validated or if the attacker has a certificate for the domain (via fraudulent CA issuance or a self-signed cert that employees bypass), employees enter their VPN credentials. (5) The attacker captures credentials and can present a 'maintenance' message or simulate authentication failure. Defenses: certificate pinning in VPN clients, DNSSEC validation, browser HSTS/HPKP.
explanations.c: VPN clients use hostname resolution for server discovery — they connect to the hostname in their configuration (corp-vpn.targetorg.com), which resolves via DNS. DNS poisoning directly intercepts this resolution, redirecting the VPN client to the attacker's server. VPN clients do NOT verify server identity solely by IP address — they use TLS certificate validation based on the hostname.
explanations.d: Certificate Authorities issue certificates based on domain control validation (DCV) — typically through DNS record validation, HTTP file placement, or email to domain contacts. DNS poisoning of a resolver cache does not grant control of the actual DNS zone or the ability to respond to CA validation challenges. Only DNS zone control (control of the authoritative nameserver) enables fraudulent certificate issuance through DNS-based DCV.

questions.name: Network and Perimeter Hacking
questions.keyword: DNS poisoning spoofing cache Kaminsky attack
questions.text: DNSSEC (DNS Security Extensions) is deployed to prevent DNS cache poisoning. Which specific mechanism does DNSSEC use to allow resolvers to verify DNS record authenticity?

answers.text: DNSSEC encrypts all DNS responses using AES-256 — resolvers decrypt responses using the zone's public key to verify the content was not modified in transit

DNSSEC digitally signs DNS resource records using asymmetric cryptography — resolvers validate the RRSIG (Resource Record Signature) using the zone's public key (DNSKEY) to verify records were signed by the legitimate zone owner and have not been tampered with
DNSSEC uses HMAC-SHA256 message authentication codes — the DNS resolver and authoritative server share a pre-configured symmetric key (TSIG) for authenticating all query-response pairs
DNSSEC uses TLS to establish an encrypted session between resolvers and authoritative servers — all DNS records are delivered over a TLS-authenticated channel preventing cache injection

explanations.a: DNSSEC does NOT encrypt DNS responses — DNS records remain in plaintext (visible to anyone who intercepts the packets). DNSSEC provides authentication (verifying records are from the legitimate zone owner and unchanged) but not confidentiality (hiding the record content). DNS over HTTPS (DoH) or DNS over TLS (DoT) provide confidentiality, but these are separate from DNSSEC.
explanations.b: DNSSEC (RFC 4033-4035) establishes a chain of trust using digital signatures: (1) Zone operators sign all resource record sets (RRsets) with their private key, creating RRSIG records. (2) Each zone's public key is published in DNSKEY records. (3) DNSKEY records are signed by the parent zone's private key, creating a chain up to the DNS root. (4) The root zone's DNSKEY is a well-known trust anchor embedded in resolvers. (5) When a DNSSEC-validating resolver receives a response, it retrieves the RRSIG and validates it against the zone's DNSKEY. (6) If the signature is valid, the record is authenticated — any tampered or injected record with an invalid signature is rejected. This prevents cache poisoning because forged records would lack valid signatures.
explanations.c: TSIG (Transaction SIGnature, RFC 2845) uses HMAC with a shared secret key to authenticate DNS transactions between specific configured pairs (e.g., primary-secondary zone transfer authentication). TSIG is used for securing zone transfers and DDNS updates between trusted parties — it requires pre-shared key configuration between specific servers and is separate from the DNSSEC public key infrastructure used for end-to-end authentication.
explanations.d: DNS over TLS (DoT, RFC 7858) establishes TLS sessions between resolvers and authoritative servers for confidentiality and transport authentication — it prevents MITM interception of DNS traffic. DoT/DoH are transport security mechanisms, separate from DNSSEC's data authentication mechanism. DNSSEC operates independently of the transport and works over standard UDP/TCP DNS.

questions.name: Network and Perimeter Hacking
questions.keyword: DNS poisoning spoofing cache Kaminsky attack
questions.text: A threat analyst investigates an incident where internal DNS queries are returning incorrect IP addresses for external websites. The internal DNS resolver has not been compromised, and DNSSEC is not deployed. Wireshark captures show DNS responses arriving 200ms before the legitimate response from the authoritative server. What attack is occurring and what does the 200ms timing indicate?

answers.text: The attack is DNS amplification DDoS — the 200ms timing indicates the attacker is timing response floods to precede legitimate server responses for maximum amplification effect

The attack is an off-path DNS cache poisoning race condition — an attacker is sending forged DNS responses to the resolver faster than legitimate responses arrive from the authoritative server, succeeding when their forged response with correct TXID arrives first within the 200ms window before the real response
The attack is BGP route hijacking — the 200ms timing indicates BGP route changes that slow legitimate DNS responses while accelerating attacker-controlled response paths
The 200ms timing is normal DNS resolver behavior — recursive resolvers always pre-cache responses 200ms before the authoritative TTL expires to ensure fresh records are available

explanations.a: DNS amplification DDoS uses open DNS resolvers to generate large responses directed at a spoofed victim IP — the attacker sends small queries with the victim's IP as the source, and the resolver sends large responses to the victim. This is a volume amplification attack, not a cache poisoning attack. The timing pattern described (responses arriving before legitimate ones) is not characteristic of amplification DDoS.
explanations.b: The 200ms early arrival is the signature of an off-path DNS cache poisoning attack in progress: (1) The attacker observes (or triggers) the resolver making a DNS query for a domain. (2) The attacker sends a flood of forged DNS responses to the resolver, each with a different guessed TXID value. (3) The attacker's responses arrive 200ms before the legitimate authoritative server's response (because the attacker's server is closer or faster, or the legitimate path is slower). (4) If any forged response has the correct TXID and source port matching the resolver's query, the resolver accepts it and caches the poisoned record. (5) The legitimate response arrives 200ms later but is rejected (the resolver already has a cached answer). The 200ms window is the timing advantage the attacker exploits — modern DNS poisoning requires both TXID guessing AND source port prediction to succeed without DNS flooding countermeasures.
explanations.c: BGP route hijacking diverts network traffic by announcing more specific or fraudulent BGP prefixes — it would slow legitimate DNS responses if the route to the authoritative server is hijacked. However, BGP hijacking would cause all traffic to the target prefixes to be affected, not just DNS, and would not result in forged DNS responses appearing before legitimate ones. The described attack is specifically a DNS-layer attack.
explanations.d: DNS resolvers do not pre-cache responses before TTL expiry through early responses — they serve cached responses until TTL expiry, then send new queries and wait for fresh responses. There is no 'pre-caching' mechanism that causes responses to arrive 200ms early. Early-arriving responses in packet captures indicate attacker-generated packets, not resolver behavior.

questions.name: Network and Perimeter Hacking
questions.keyword: sniffing tools Wireshark tcpdump network analysis
questions.text: A network security analyst uses tcpdump on a Linux system to capture only HTTP traffic. Which tcpdump command correctly captures TCP traffic on port 80 from a specific host (192.168.1.50)?

answers.text: tcpdump -i eth0 host 192.168.1.50 and tcp port 80 — captures TCP port 80 traffic to/from 192.168.1.50
tcpdump --interface=eth0 --filter='http' --host=192.168.1.50 — uses long-form HTTP protocol filter and host specification
tcpdump -i eth0 ip 192.168.1.50 http-port — uses IP and HTTP port keywords specific to the HTTP filter module
tcpdump -i eth0 capture=80 source=192.168.1.50 — assigns port and source using key=value syntax

explanations.a: tcpdump uses Berkeley Packet Filter (BPF) syntax for filtering. The correct command: '-i eth0' specifies the capture interface, 'host 192.168.1.50' matches packets where the source OR destination IP is 192.168.1.50, 'and' is the logical AND operator in BPF, 'tcp port 80' matches TCP packets with source or destination port 80. Combined: captures all TCP port 80 (HTTP) traffic involving 192.168.1.50. Additional useful variants: 'src host 192.168.1.50 and tcp dst port 80' (only outbound HTTP requests from the host); '-w capture.pcap' to save to file; '-A' to print packet ASCII content.
explanations.b: tcpdump does not support '--filter=http' (there is no HTTP-specific filter keyword in BPF — HTTP is application layer, and BPF filters at lower layers). '--host=' is not valid tcpdump syntax — long-form flags use double dashes only for certain options (-i has --interface). The correct filter syntax uses positional BPF expressions, not key=value pairs.
explanations.c: 'ip 192.168.1.50' is not valid BPF syntax (should be 'host' or 'src/dst host'). 'http-port' is not a BPF primitive — BPF uses 'port 80' or 'port http' (where http is a named service). This command would produce a tcpdump parse error.
explanations.d: tcpdump uses no 'capture=' or 'source=' key=value syntax — all filters are BPF expressions using protocol keywords, qualifiers, and primitives. 'source=192.168.1.50' is not valid BPF syntax. tcpdump's options are specified with flags (-i, -n, -v, -w, etc.), not key=value pairs.

questions.name: Network and Perimeter Hacking
questions.keyword: sniffing tools Wireshark tcpdump network analysis
questions.text: A security analyst captures network traffic with Wireshark and wants to find all HTTP POST requests containing the string 'password' in the packet body. Which Wireshark display filter correctly isolates these packets?

answers.text: http.request.method == 'POST' and frame contains 'password' — filters HTTP POST requests where any part of the frame contains the string 'password'
tcp.port == 80 and data.text == 'password' — filters TCP port 80 packets where the data payload is exactly the string 'password'
ip.proto == 6 and payload contains 'POST' — filters IPv4 TCP packets containing the POST string anywhere in the payload
http.method = POST and grep 'password' — uses HTTP method filter combined with shell grep for string matching

explanations.a: Wireshark display filters use protocol-specific field names: 'http.request.method == "POST"' — matches HTTP request packets where the method is POST (alternative syntax: http.request.method == POST without quotes also works in newer versions). 'frame contains "password"' — searches all bytes in the entire frame for the ASCII string 'password'. Combined with 'and', this filter returns only HTTP POST packets containing 'password' anywhere (headers or body). Alternatively: 'http.request.method == POST and http.file_data contains "password"' to specifically search the HTTP body/form data fields.
explanations.b: 'data.text == "password"' in Wireshark matches only packets where the DATA layer content exactly equals 'password' — not where it contains 'password' as a substring. For containment, 'contains' or 'matches' operators are needed. Additionally, 'data.text' is a raw data field that may not correctly represent HTTP POST body content.
explanations.c: 'ip.proto == 6' is equivalent to filtering for TCP (protocol 6) but uses the raw IP protocol number — less readable than 'tcp'. More critically, 'payload contains "POST"' is not a standard Wireshark display filter field. The correct contains syntax uses specific protocol fields or 'frame contains'.
explanations.d: Wireshark display filters do not support grep — grep is a command-line tool for text search in files, not a Wireshark filter function. 'http.method' is not standard Wireshark field syntax (should be 'http.request.method'). The 'and grep' construct would cause a Wireshark filter syntax error.

questions.name: Network and Perimeter Hacking
questions.keyword: sniffing tools Wireshark tcpdump network analysis
questions.text: A penetration tester captures a pcap file containing FTP session traffic between a server (10.0.0.5) and a client. When analyzing the capture in Wireshark, which feature allows the tester to reconstruct the complete FTP command and data exchange including any transferred files?

answers.text: Wireshark's 'Export Packets' feature — exports all packets in the FTP session to a text file for external analysis
Wireshark's 'Follow TCP Stream' feature — reconstructs the complete TCP session content by reassembling all TCP segments, displaying both directions of the FTP control and data channel exchange
Wireshark's 'Decode As' feature — converts FTP packets to HTTP format for analysis in standard web debugging tools
Wireshark's 'Colorize Conversation' feature — color-codes FTP packets to make it easier to identify credential-containing frames manually

explanations.a: 'Export Packets' exports selected packets to a new pcap file for sharing or focused analysis — it preserves the raw packet format and does not reconstruct the session payload or reassemble TCP streams.
explanations.b: Wireshark's 'Follow TCP Stream' (right-click on any FTP packet → Follow → TCP Stream) reassembles all TCP segments from both directions of a TCP connection and displays the raw payload as a readable conversation. For FTP control channel (port 21): shows the complete command exchange including USER, PASS (credentials in plaintext!), RETR/STOR commands (files transferred), and server responses. For FTP data channel (port 20 or passive ports): shows the actual file content being transferred. This feature is essential for credential extraction from unencrypted protocols (FTP, Telnet, HTTP, POP3, SMTP).
explanations.c: 'Decode As' allows Wireshark to interpret packets using a different protocol dissector — for example, interpreting traffic on a non-standard port as HTTP. It does not convert FTP to HTTP format or enable web debugging tool compatibility. FTP has its own dissector that already correctly interprets FTP protocol messages.
explanations.d: 'Colorize Conversation' applies color highlighting to all packets belonging to the same conversation — useful for visually distinguishing multiple simultaneous connections in a busy capture. It does not reconstruct session content, reassemble TCP streams, or identify credential frames. It is a display aid, not a content analysis tool.

questions.name: Network and Perimeter Hacking
questions.keyword: sniffing tools Wireshark tcpdump network analysis
questions.text: A security analyst reviews a pcap file and observes thousands of TCP SYN packets from source IP 192.168.1.200 targeting 192.168.2.50 on sequential ports (1, 2, 3, 4, 5... up to 65535) at 10ms intervals, with NO corresponding SYN-ACK or RST responses visible for most ports. What activity does this traffic pattern definitively indicate?

answers.text: Normal server health check traffic — servers continuously probe their own listening ports at regular intervals to verify service availability

TCP SYN port scanning — the sequential port coverage, 10ms inter-packet timing, single-direction SYN flow, and lack of complete handshakes are signature characteristics of a systematic Nmap-style SYN scan from 192.168.1.200 against 192.168.2.50
A TCP SYN flood DDoS attack — sequential port scanning with 10ms intervals indicates the attacker is deliberately overwhelming the target's TCP connection queue one port at a time
BGP route convergence traffic — BGP path updates after a network topology change use sequential TCP port probing to verify end-to-end connectivity across all potential routing paths

explanations.a: Server health checks (heartbeat packets) use specific well-known service ports for known services — they do not sequentially probe all 65,535 ports. Health check traffic is periodic for specific services (e.g., TCP connection to port 80 every 30 seconds), not sequential sequential sweeps at uniform millisecond intervals.
explanations.b: This traffic pattern has multiple signatures of systematic port scanning: (1) Sequential port progression (1, 2, 3, 4...) — methodical coverage of all port numbers as Nmap would do with '-p 1-65535'. (2) 10ms inter-packet timing — consistent, programmatic timing is characteristic of automated scanning tools (Nmap -T3 uses similar intervals). (3) Single source to single destination — targeted host scanning, not network-wide discovery. (4) SYN-only without complete handshakes — a TCP SYN scan (-sS) sends SYN probes and immediately RSTs SYN-ACK responses without completing the handshake. Ports returning RST (closed) and no response (filtered) dominate the capture. (5) Coverage of all 65,535 ports — comprehensive enumeration. This is definitively port scanning reconnaissance, most likely 'nmap -sS -p 1-65535 192.168.2.50' from 192.168.1.200.
explanations.c: SYN flood DDoS attacks target a single port or small set of ports with massive SYN volume to exhaust TCP connection state on the victim — they do not sequentially progress through all 65,535 ports. SYN floods aim to overwhelm connection tables with many half-open connections on one port; port scanning aims to map service availability across all ports.
explanations.d: BGP is a routing protocol operating on TCP port 179 between BGP peers — it does not use sequential port probing for route convergence. BGP sends UPDATE messages to neighboring routers using established BGP sessions on port 179. BGP has no mechanism involving scanning sequential TCP ports.

questions.name: Network and Perimeter Hacking
questions.keyword: sniffing countermeasures detection prevention encryption
questions.text: Which network security countermeasure MOST fundamentally renders passive network sniffing ineffective against capturing usable credential data?

answers.text: Deploying a dedicated network intrusion detection system (NIDS) on all segments — NIDS alerts when sniffing tools are detected, enabling rapid security response
Using switched network infrastructure (replacing hubs with managed switches) — switches prevent promiscuous mode from capturing traffic not addressed to the sniffer's port

Encrypting all sensitive communications using strong protocols (TLS/HTTPS, SSH, SFTP, S/MIME) — even if traffic is captured, encrypted content is cryptographically protected and useless to the attacker without the session keys
Implementing 802.1Q VLAN segmentation — VLANs create separate broadcast domains that prevent sniffers from seeing traffic in other VLANs

explanations.a: NIDS detecting sniffing activity provides detective capability — alerting when sniffers are active. However, NIDS detection does not prevent data capture or protect captured data content. An attacker who captures data before detection still has whatever they captured. Detection is reactive; encryption is preventive.
explanations.b: Switched networks prevent passive sniffing of traffic not addressed to the attacker's port — requiring active attacks (ARP poisoning) to intercept other hosts' traffic. However, active sniffing (ARP poisoning MITM) still captures traffic on switched networks. This is a useful control but not the most fundamental defense against all sniffing.
explanations.c: End-to-end encryption is the most fundamental defense because it renders captured data useless regardless of how it was captured: (1) TLS/HTTPS protects web application credentials, session cookies, and data in transit. (2) SSH protects remote administration sessions instead of Telnet. (3) SFTP/FTPS protects file transfer credentials instead of FTP. (4) S/MIME or PGP protects email content. (5) VPN encrypts all traffic across network segments. Even if an attacker successfully performs ARP poisoning on a switched network and captures the complete TCP stream, they see only ciphertext without the session keys. Encryption protects against passive sniffing, active MITM sniffing (without certificate interception), and retrospective analysis of captured packets.
explanations.d: VLAN segmentation creates separate Layer 2 broadcast domains — hosts in VLAN 10 cannot directly sniff traffic in VLAN 20 without routing between them. However, VLANs do not prevent sniffing within the same VLAN, and VLAN hopping attacks (double-tagging, switch spoofing) can potentially cross VLAN boundaries. VLANs are a useful containment measure but not the most fundamental protection for sensitive data.

questions.name: Network and Perimeter Hacking
questions.keyword: sniffing countermeasures detection prevention encryption
questions.text: A network security team wants to detect hosts running packet sniffers in promiscuous mode on their LAN segment. Which detection technique leverages a behavior specific to promiscuous mode NICs?

answers.text: Ping the broadcast address — hosts in promiscuous mode respond to broadcast pings with additional ICMP echo reply packets not seen from normal-mode hosts

Send specially crafted Ethernet frames with a non-broadcast destination MAC that no host 'should' receive and process (since their NICs should drop it) — a host in promiscuous mode that processes and responds to such frames reveals its promiscuous state
Monitor for ARP cache entries — hosts in promiscuous mode automatically create ARP cache entries for all observed hosts, and querying their ARP table reveals traffic interception
Send DNS queries containing the word 'sniffer' — promiscuous mode NICs forward these queries to the OS which generates distinctive DNS error responses detectable by monitoring

explanations.a: All hosts respond to ICMP echo requests (pings) addressed to the broadcast address — this is standard IP behavior unrelated to promiscuous mode. Promiscuous mode does not change ICMP broadcast response behavior. Normal-mode hosts also respond to directed broadcasts in many configurations.
explanations.b: A classic promiscuous mode detection technique uses non-broadcast, non-local MAC addresses: (1) The detector sends an ICMP echo request (ping) with a unicast IP address targeting a specific suspect host, but with a deliberately WRONG destination MAC address (e.g., a randomly generated MAC that doesn't belong to any host). (2) A normal-mode NIC would silently discard this frame because the destination MAC doesn't match its own MAC — the frame never reaches the IP layer. (3) A promiscuous-mode NIC passes all frames to the OS regardless of destination MAC — the IP stack receives the ICMP echo request and processes it, potentially generating an ICMP echo reply. (4) The reply reveals that the host processed a frame it should have discarded — indicating promiscuous mode. Tools like Sentinel, AntiSniff, and Promiscdetect use variations of this technique.
explanations.c: ARP caches are populated by observing ARP broadcasts and ARP replies — all hosts on a segment maintain ARP entries for recently communicated hosts, regardless of promiscuous mode. Promiscuous mode does not automatically create ARP cache entries for all observed traffic; the ARP cache is managed by the IP/ARP stack based on addressed ARP packets, not by the NIC's MAC filter state.
explanations.d: DNS queries with specific content generate DNS protocol errors based on the query type and domain name — not based on the NIC's promiscuous mode state. DNS servers process queries based on their configuration, not on the promiscuous mode of any hosts on the network. This is a fabricated detection technique.

questions.name: Network and Perimeter Hacking
questions.keyword: sniffing countermeasures detection prevention encryption
questions.text: An organization replaces all legacy Telnet and FTP administrative access with SSH and SFTP. Additionally, they deploy HTTPS-only for all internal web applications. A network sniffer captures all traffic on the segment. What data can the sniffer realistically extract from the captured traffic?

answers.text: All credentials and data — SSH and HTTPS encryption is automatically disabled in corporate network environments where the administrator has not explicitly enabled encryption through group policy
No useful data — end-to-end encryption prevents any intelligence extraction from captured network traffic in all scenarios

Traffic metadata (source/destination IPs, ports, packet sizes, timing, connection duration, DNS queries) but NOT application payload content — encryption protects the data content while leaving network metadata visible
Only ICMP traffic — switches ensure that SSH and HTTPS traffic is never forwarded to sniffer ports regardless of promiscuous mode settings

explanations.a: SSH and HTTPS use strong cryptographic protocols — SSH uses Diffie-Hellman key exchange and AES encryption; HTTPS uses TLS 1.2/1.3 with Perfect Forward Secrecy. These are not disabled by corporate network policy or group policy. The encryption is enforced at the cryptographic protocol level, not by network policy.
explanations.b: Encryption protects payload content but does not prevent all intelligence extraction. Even from encrypted traffic, network metadata provides significant intelligence: which IP addresses communicate (who talks to whom), which ports (services used), how often (usage patterns), when (working hours, anomalous off-hours activity), how much data (large uploads may indicate exfiltration). DNS queries (unless DoH is deployed) reveal which domains are accessed. TLS handshakes reveal the SNI (Server Name Indication) which discloses the target domain. Traffic analysis (machine learning on metadata) can infer application behavior even from encrypted streams.
explanations.c: End-to-end encryption protects the confidentiality of application data within the encrypted session. The network layer metadata (IP headers, TCP/UDP headers, timing, DNS) remains visible to a network sniffer. From encrypted traffic, a sniffer can observe: source/destination IP addresses, TCP/UDP ports (service type), packet sizes and timing (traffic fingerprinting), DNS queries/responses (revealing domain names accessed unless DoH is used), TLS SNI (Server Name Indication) revealing target domain, certificate exchange (revealing server identity and CA), and connection duration and data volume.
explanations.d: SSH and HTTPS traffic IS forwarded to all ports in normal switch operation (unicast forwarding), and to all ports in promiscuous mode — switches do not specially handle encrypted traffic differently from unencrypted traffic at the frame forwarding level. The switch forwards frames to the port that learned the destination MAC, regardless of whether the payload is SSH, HTTPS, or plaintext.

questions.name: Network and Perimeter Hacking
questions.keyword: sniffing countermeasures detection prevention encryption
questions.text: A security team discovers evidence that an insider has been conducting packet sniffing on a critical internal network segment for 3 months. During this period, all administrative access used SSH, all web applications used HTTPS, and internal databases used TLS client certificates. The insider did not have access to private keys. What intelligence could the insider realistically have gathered despite these encryption controls?

answers.text: No intelligence — the combination of SSH, HTTPS, and TLS certificate authentication is a complete security solution that prevents any intelligence gathering from network traffic
The insider could have captured complete plaintext credentials and session data — SSH and TLS are trivially defeated by a local network sniffer with administrative privileges

The insider could have gathered: communication patterns (who communicates with what systems, frequency, volume), DNS query logs revealing accessed internal services and external domains (if DNS is not encrypted), TLS SNI revealing web application hostnames accessed, failed authentication patterns (from TCP reset patterns), timing analysis of administrative sessions, and network topology information from routing and ARP traffic
The insider could only have captured ICMP traffic — encrypted protocols prevent NICs from processing any TCP or UDP frames in promiscuous mode

explanations.a: Even with comprehensive encryption, significant intelligence remains extractable from network metadata. The claim of 'complete security' from encryption alone ignores the substantial intelligence value of traffic analysis — a well-documented intelligence discipline even against nation-state encrypted communications.
explanations.b: SSH and TLS with certificate authentication provide strong cryptographic protection for payload data. An insider without access to private keys cannot decrypt SSH sessions or TLS-protected application data from captured traffic. The claim of 'trivially defeated' is incorrect for properly implemented modern cryptography.
explanations.c: Three months of packet captures, even from entirely encrypted sessions, yield substantial intelligence through metadata analysis: (1) Communication patterns — which internal IPs communicate with which systems, at what times, for how long, revealing application dependencies and user behavioral patterns.
